title: Three Ways to Lead a Boys' Club
text:
In the late 1930s Kurt Lewin and his students Ronald Lippitt and Ralph White formed small after-school clubs of ten and eleven year old boys in Iowa. The boys made masks, painted and built things. Adult leaders were trained to lead in one of three styles, and they rotated between clubs so that personality did not explain the results.

The autocratic leader decided everything, handed out tasks step by step and praised or criticized without explaining why. The democratic leader let the group discuss and choose its projects and offered options and reasons. The laissez-faire leader stayed friendly but passive and left the boys to themselves.

The differences were striking. Under autocratic leaders, groups either became apathetic or showed much more hostility, often taking it out on a scapegoat. Work went on while the leader was in the room, but when he stepped out, it largely stopped. Under democratic leaders the boys were friendlier, more creative and kept working when the leader left. The laissez-faire groups got the least done. Most boys said they preferred the democratic leader.
lesson: Control can keep people busy while you watch. Involving them in decisions keeps them working when you are not there.
people: Kurt Lewin, Ronald Lippitt, Ralph White
location: University of Iowa, Iowa City, USA
source: Lewin, K., Lippitt, R., and White, R. K. (1939). Patterns of aggressive behavior in experimentally created 'social climates.' Journal of Social Psychology, 10(2), 271-299.
caveat: The groups were few and small, so the results are best read as a vivid early demonstration rather than a precise measurement.
place: University of Iowa, Iowa City, USA
